job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817 (as amended Oct. 6, 2026): Drafting Problems, Loopholes, and Vulnerabilities

This review covers only the text you pasted. I haven't checked it against the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (DSHMRA), NOAA's implementing rules, or the committee report, so counsel should verify the legal-challenge items.

## Scope and definitions (Sec. 2)

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A), single-vessel threshold.** Tonnage is counted per vessel, with no aggregation rule for affiliates or common control. An operator could split recovery across several vessels, or rotate them, each under 10,000 t/yr, and stay outside the definition.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "per year" and unit of measure.** The text doesn't say whether the year is calendar or rolling, whether tons are wet or dry (nodules carry substantial moisture), or who measures. A short high-rate campaign or partial-year operation could fall under the line, and the government would struggle to prove the threshold was crossed.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "recovery" and "by a single vessel."** "Recovery" isn't defined, so it's unclear whether it means collection on the seafloor, lift through a riser, or transfer to a surface vessel. Recovery by a non-vessel platform or autonomous seabed system, or tonnage handed between vessels, may not be attributable to any "single vessel."

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "200 meters" and "other mineral resources."** 200 m is far shallower than the usual meaning of "deep seabed," and no geographic limit is stated. "Mineral resources" is undefined, so the text arguably reaches oil and gas, sand and gravel, or other offshore activity, which invites vagueness and overbreadth arguments.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(B), Secretary's determination.** "Secretary" is undefined (Sec. 6 names the Secretary of State, so the omission here looks like a drafting error). There is no standard beyond "comparable" risks, no rulemaking, notice, or publication requirement, and no statement of whether it applies to pre-determination conduct. Because violations carry criminal penalties, this invites fair-notice, vagueness, and nondelegation challenges.

6. **Sec. 2(2), "U.S. person."** It covers only citizens and "corporations organized under the laws of a State." It omits LLCs, partnerships, trusts, joint ventures, permanent residents, and DC, territorial, or federally chartered entities ("State" is undefined). It has no control test for foreign subsidiaries, so restructuring could take an operator outside the definition.

7. **Sec. 2(3), "covered vessel."** The 5,000 gross ton threshold is unrelated to the 10,000 t/yr threshold, so a smaller vessel could exceed the recovery threshold without being a covered vessel. "Equipped for" is ambiguous for temporary or chartered equipment, and the tonnage convention isn't specified.

## Prohibition and exemptions (Sec. 3)

8. **Sec. 3(a), jurisdictional reach.** "In the United States" is undefined (territorial sea? EEZ? OCS?). The prohibition doesn't reach foreign persons or foreign-flag vessels operating abroad, and there is no US-flag hook. Foreign-incorporated affiliates operating overseas fall outside it.

9. **Sec. 3(a), only recovery is prohibited.** Nothing bars processing, importing, purchasing, financing, transporting, or taking offtake of nodules, and there is no aiding-and-abetting or conspiracy language. US firms could still finance or process material recovered by uncovered entities abroad. "Engage" is also undefined.

10. **Sec. 3(b), "exploration license" is undefined.** The text doesn't say who must issue it: NOAA under DSHMRA, the International Seabed Authority, or a foreign sponsoring state. Either reading produces a dispute. Exploration licenses don't ordinarily authorize commercial-scale recovery, yet the clause exempts "mining conducted under" them with no tonnage cap.

11. **Sec. 3(b), grandfathering has no limits.** There is no expiration, area or volume limit, or treatment of renewals, amendments, transfers to affiliates, or successors. A licensee could argue the exemption lasts as long as the license, however modified.

12. **Sec. 3(b), who is and isn't protected.** Only exploration licensees are exempted. Holders of DSHMRA commercial recovery permits, pending applicants, and investors mid-development get nothing, which creates a cliff at enactment and a likely litigation target (see item 24).

13. **Sec. 3(c), environmental assessment exemption.** The term is undefined, and there is no limit on scale, duration, tonnage, or what happens to recovered material. The test is the "purpose" of the activity, which is subjective and hard to disprove, and the burden of proof isn't allocated. Dual-purpose "test mining" is probably the largest practical loophole in the bill.

14. **Whole bill, relationship to DSHMRA (30 U.S.C. § 1401 et seq.).** The bill neither amends nor repeals DSHMRA and has no "notwithstanding" clause. As drafted, NOAA could keep issuing licenses and permits for activity this Act makes unlawful, which invites reliance and estoppel claims and conflicting-authority litigation.

## Registry and enforcement (Secs. 4–5)

15. **Sec. 4, no penalty attaches.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of section 3. Failing to register or filing late or inaccurate reports has no specific consequence (only general false-statement law, e.g., 18 U.S.C. § 1001, might apply), and there is no deadline for registration or the first report.

16. **Sec. 4, "operator" and implementation gaps.** "Operator" is undefined (owner, charterer, contractor?). The section gives NOAA no rulemaking authority, no report content requirements (tonnage, location), no audit, inspection, or verification power, no authority to deny or revoke registration, and no confidentiality protections. Reports may not establish whether the threshold was crossed.

17. **Sec. 5(a), no enforcement machinery.** No agency is designated to assess penalties, and there is no administrative process, Attorney General civil action, injunctive relief, seizure or forfeiture authority, or boarding and inspection power. Detecting and proving offshore activity, especially on the high seas, is left entirely unaddressed.

18. **Sec. 5(a), "each day" against an annual threshold.** The violation turns on annual tonnage, so it's unclear on what day a violation begins and whether each later day is a separate violation. That creates proof and calculation problems.

19. **Sec. 5(a) vs. Sec. 8, retroactivity conflict.** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act doesn't take effect until 180 days later. It's unclear whether conduct during the gap is punishable, which invites fair-notice and retroactivity challenges.

20. **Sec. 5(a), penalty size.** $1,000,000 per day has no stated factors, proportionality guidance, or ability-to-pay consideration, and it is exposed to an Eighth Amendment Excessive Fines challenge.

21. **Sec. 5(b), "willfully" and criminal exposure.** "Willfully" is undefined, and the offense rests on unclear terms (items 5, 10, and 13). Defendants will have strong lack-of-knowledge and rule-of-lenity arguments against a 10-year maximum. Corporate and officer liability aren't addressed.

## Duration, timing, and structure (Secs. 6–8)

22. **Sec. 6, international agreement.** "Shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months" is ambiguous about whether the deadline applies to starting or concluding talks. There is no reporting requirement, consequence, definition of "equivalent," or mention of Senate advice and consent, so the section is effectively hortatory.

23. **Sec. 7, internal contradiction and a weak lift mechanism.** 7(a) says the prohibition continues until Congress acts, while 7(b) ends the Act after 10 years regardless. The sunset is measured from enactment rather than the effective date, and there is no savings clause for pending enforcement. 7(a) also has no trigger, deadline, or funding for the NASEM report, no definition of "serious harm," and no expedited procedure for a joint resolution that is subject to veto and filibuster.

24. **Sec. 8, 180-day gap.** Nothing restricts ramp-up, new agency authorizations, or contracting during the gap, and there is no wind-down or transition provision for operations in progress. The registry start date is also unspecified.

25. **Whole bill, structural omissions.** There is no severability clause (so a successful challenge to 2(1)(B), for example, raises the question of whether the rest survives), no general rulemaking authority, no judicial review provisions, and no authorization of appropriations.

26. **Sec. 3 generally, takings, due process, and international law.** Prohibiting activity by permit holders, applicants, and investors with no compensation or transition invites Fifth Amendment takings and due process claims. Applying the prohibition to US persons on the high seas may also draw freedom-of-the-seas arguments. Outcomes on either are uncertain.

## Suggested emphasis

- **Strongest "companies keep going" items:** 1, 3, 6, 8, 10–11, and 13, plus 9 (processing and financing aren't covered).
- **Strongest "hard to enforce" items:** 15–17 and 18.
- **Strongest "easy to challenge" items:** 5, 19, 21, and 26, plus 25 (no severability).

One strategic point for the policy team: many of these are fixable by a manager's amendment, so raising them in committee could help the sponsors tighten the bill. The vagueness, retroactivity, and takings points carry more weight in litigation or in a pitch for a narrower approach. It may be worth deciding which issues to raise publicly and which to hold for later.

If useful, I can turn this into a one-page memo for members' staff or draft proposed amendment language or questions for the markup.
